layers.title: Castle rock
layers.intro: The sandstone rock at the west end of the old town: the castle, the passages and caves beneath it, the inns at its foot and the statues in its grounds.

layers.title: Market Square
layers.intro: The Old Market Square, where the two medieval towns met, and the streets around it: the town's Exchange and the Council House that replaced it, old inns, a library, theatres and halls.

groups.title: The market
groups.intro: The square where the two medieval towns met: its market and Goose Fair, St Peter's, the frame-knitting trade, old inns, the Exchange and the Council House that replaced it.

groups.title: Houses, hotels and halls
groups.intro: Around the square: a Georgian house with its library, theatres, a hotel, concert and music halls, and a skating rink that became Rock City.

layers.title: Lace Market
layers.intro: The old Saxon town on its hill east of the square, where lace merchants built their warehouses, and the low ground below it towards the canal and the station.

layers.title: North of the centre
layers.intro: The hills north of the old town, built over in the 19th century: parks and cemeteries, a cathedral, a college and a railway station.

layers.title: Sneinton
layers.intro: The hill east of the city: a windmill, cave dwellings, a church by Thomas Rickman, the old wholesale market and the later laboratory of the Boots team that discovered ibuprofen.

layers.title: St Ann's
layers.intro: The hill north-east of the old town: a healing well, the oldest allotments in England, the terraces of New Town, and the estate that replaced them.

layers.title: The Meadows
layers.intro: The low ground between the city and the Trent, with two football grounds facing each other across the river, and a flood.

layers.title: Hockley
layers.intro: The old Walker Gate below the Lace Market: cloth, chapels and cotton, the first Boots shop, cinemas, and the city's bus depot.

groups.title: Hockley
items: Pulp Fiction and the Screen Room

layers.title: The Park Estate
layers.intro: The castle's old deer park, built over with Victorian villas and still lit by gas.

groups.title: The Park Estate
items: Sold, saved and run by its residents

layers.title: Castle Marina
layers.intro: The Nottingham Canal west of the town: wharves and warehouses on Canal Street, and a marina on old railway sidings.

layers.title: Wilford
layers.intro: A village on the south bank of the Trent, reached for centuries by ferry and, since the 1870s, by bridge.

groups.title: Ford, manor and church
groups.intro: The oldest Wilford: a Roman ford in the Trent, the manor in Domesday Book, and St Wilfrid's Church.

groups.title: The village and its big house
groups.intro: The village of the 17th to the early 19th century: its inn, Wilford House, a sea captain, a poet and the Nottingham Captain.

groups.title: Bridges, coal and the suburb
groups.intro: From 1868 a colliery, toll and suspension bridges and a power station, as the village grew into a suburb.

groups.title: Sportsmen of Wilford
groups.intro: Three footballers born or living in Wilford, two of them Iremongers.

groups.title: War and the trams
groups.intro: War graves in the churchyard, and the trams that reached Wilford in 2015.

layers.title: West Bridgford
layers.intro: South of the river: Test cricket, Nottingham Forest and the county's headquarters.

groups.title: Trent Bridge
groups.intro: From a fort of the 920s and a medieval stone bridge to Test cricket, Nottingham Forest's ground and County Hall, all at the south end of Trent Bridge.

groups.title: Bridgford & Lady Bay
groups.intro: The old village round St Giles', the estate said to have been won at cards, the railway bridge at Lady Bay, wartime bombs, the 1947 flood and a superstore.

groups.title: Edwalton
groups.intro: A village with a 12th-century church and a railway station, and Compton Acres, built mostly in the 1990s.

layers.title: Clifton
layers.intro: An old village above the Trent, and next to it one of the largest housing estates ever built by a council.

groups.title: The village
items: The thatched houses of Village Road
groups.intro: The old village on the hill above the Trent: its 12th-century church, the Cliftons' hall, thatched houses, almshouses, a dovecote and the school.

groups.title: Clifton Grove
groups.intro: Along the river below the village: a Bronze Age settlement, the avenue of elms, a ballad of a jilted lover, and the bridge of 1958.

groups.title: The estate and its people
groups.intro: Beside the old village the council built one of its largest estates from the 1950s, and two sporting names came from here.

layers.title: Barton in Fabis
layers.intro: A village on the south bank of the Trent, upstream from Clifton, once called Barton in the Beans: its medieval church, a dovecote of 1677, and the new district of Fairham.

layers.title: Thrumpton
layers.intro: A small estate village on the Trent: its Jacobean hall and the families who owned it, its church, and the houses built for the estate.

layers.title: Ruddington
layers.intro: A village of framework knitters south of the city, the Second World War ammunition depot beyond it, the site of Flawford's lost church, whose name the village church took, and a Victorian banker's hall.

layers.title: Gotham
layers.intro: The village of the Wise Men: its church, the name that travelled to New York and Batman, its gypsum, and the day a tornado hit it.

layers.title: Ratcliffe-on-Soar
layers.intro: By the Soar, the power station that ended coal power in Britain, and the main-line station beside it.

layers.title: Holme Pierrepont
layers.intro: The flat land along the Trent east of the city: seven centuries of Pierreponts, their Tudor brick hall and church, a power station refused, and the gravel pits that became a centre for watersports.

groups.title: Holme Pierrepont
items: The power station that was not built

layers.title: Shelford
layers.intro: A village on the Trent: its priory church and the Stanhopes, and the Royalist garrison stormed in the Civil War.

layers.title: Tollerton
layers.intro: A 12th-century church, a hall that became a seminary, and one of Britain's first municipal airfields.

layers.title: Cotgrave
layers.intro: An Anglo-Saxon burial ground, a 12th-century church, and a village that grew several times over when its colliery came.

layers.title: Radford
layers.intro: West of the centre: an old church, Raleigh's bicycles and Player's tobacco, and the streets of Saturday Night and Sunday Morning.

layers.title: Lenton
layers.intro: A Cluniac priory, dissolved in 1538, and its fair; Raleigh's works on Faraday Road, and the university at Highfields, where the MRI scanner was developed.

layers.title: Wollaton
layers.intro: The Willoughbys' village: its church and dovecote, their Elizabethan hall, the wooden wagonway from the Strelley pits, described as the first railway in Britain, and the colliery that outlasted them.

layers.title: Beeston
layers.intro: Humber's bicycle works, a silk mill burned in the Reform riots, and Boots' factories.

layers.title: Chilwell
layers.intro: A hamlet on the Ashby road that grew into a suburb, and the shell factory of the First World War.

layers.title: Giltbrook
layers.intro: Forty Bridges, the lost railway viaduct, and where the Pentrich marchers of 1817 met the soldiers and scattered.

layers.title: Eastwood
layers.intro: The mining town where coal owners planned a railway in an inn, and where D. H. Lawrence was born.

groups.title: Eastwood
items: The railway that began in a pub

layers.title: Bennerley
layers.intro: The ironworks and the iron viaduct of the Erewash valley, on ground undermined by coal workings.

layers.title: Attenborough
layers.intro: The village by the Trent: its Saxon name, a general of the Civil War, the memorial to the Chilwell dead, and the gravel pits that became a nature reserve.

layers.title: Stapleford
layers.intro: An Anglo-Saxon cross in a medieval churchyard, and a sandstone pillar on the hill full of legends.

layers.title: Arnold
layers.intro: A Domesday village and its church, a cotton mill and its house, a painter and a water engineer born here, the first Luddites, a brewery and a market.

layers.title: Calverton
layers.intro: The village of William Lee, who invented the stocking frame, and of the colliery that grew it fourfold.

layers.title: Gedling
layers.intro: A village church with a famous spire, a colliery that became a country park, a closed station and the woods of Gedling House.

layers.title: Bestwood
layers.intro: A royal hunting park, the Dukes of St Albans' lodge, and the colliery and ironworks that made a village.

layers.title: Papplewick
layers.intro: Cotton mills on the Leen, a Georgian hall, and the pumping station that brought Nottingham its water.

layers.title: Hucknall
layers.intro: The town at the north edge of the map: the church where the Byrons lie, its pits, the airfield where Rolls-Royce tested engines, and the end of the first tram line.

layers.title: Basford
layers.intro: A Domesday village on the Leen that bleached, brewed and bottled sauce.

layers.title: Bulwell
layers.intro: A market town on the Leen: its stone, its covered stalls, its hall, and the Bogs its people claimed.

layers.title: Sherwood
layers.intro: A suburb along Mansfield Road: a Georgian house, a tram depot, and a bleacher's grange that became a park.

layers.title: Mapperley
layers.intro: The hill north-east of the town: a medieval name, the Wrights' estate, two asylums, a church and the brickworks.

layers.title: Carlton
layers.intro: A township of framework knitters that the railway turned into a suburb, with an earl's church and a brickworks on the hill.

layers.title: People
layers.intro: People connected with buildings on the map: who designed them, who lived, worked or played in them, and who is remembered on their walls. Entries come from commemorative plaques (Open Plaques), architects recorded in Wikidata, and hand-written entries checked against Wikipedia and Historic England.

layers.title: Long Eaton
layers.intro: A Domesday village by the Erewash that the railway and the lace mills turned into a town.

groups.title: Long Eaton
items: The Great Fire of Long Eaton

layers.title: Ilkeston
layers.intro: A hill town over the Erewash: its charter fair, its ironworks, and the station it waited fifty years for.

layers.title: Names and beginnings
layers.intro: How the places on the map began and got their names: Bronze Age and Roman finds, Saxon burials, a cross and a fort, the villages Domesday Book wrote down in 1086, and names given since.

groups.title: Before the Normans
groups.intro: The oldest traces: a Bronze Age settlement on piles, a Roman ford, an Anglo-Saxon burial ground, the Danes who took the town in 868, and an Anglo-Saxon cross.

groups.title: In Domesday Book
groups.intro: In 1086 Domesday Book recorded many of the villages round Nottingham, some under names we would barely know.

groups.title: Names given since
groups.intro: Other names came later, from the cloth trade, a healing spring, a local official or a legend.

layers.title: Castle and Crown
layers.intro: Kings and the castle on the rock: a favourite seized in 1330, Charles I's call to arms in 1642, the Parliamentary governor who held it, the dukes' mansion that replaced it, and the riot that burned it.

groups.title: The medieval castle
groups.intro: For centuries the castle was a royal fortress, and the hunting lands round it belonged to the Crown. The stories here run from Robin Hood and the secret tunnel of 1330, by way of the deer parks and Edward IV's new tower, to the castle's decay under the Tudors.

groups.title: The Civil War
groups.intro: In August 1642 Charles I raised his standard outside the castle. Parliament then held it, under Colonel John Hutchinson, through years of Royalist raids from Newark.

groups.title: The dukes' mansion
groups.intro: After the Civil War the ruined castle was bought by the Duke of Newcastle and rebuilt as a mansion, which a crowd burned in the Reform riots of 1831, and its shell stood empty for over forty years.

groups.title: The castle museum
groups.intro: From 1878 the mansion was a museum and art gallery, and its gardens hold a memorial to the airman Albert Ball.

layers.title: The Civil War
layers.intro: Nottingham in the Civil War: where the King raised his standard, the castle held for Parliament through raid after raid, a church destroyed in the fighting, a Royalist house stormed and burned, and Shelford's church tower held by Royalists led by a woman.

groups.title: The King's standard
groups.intro: In August 1642 Charles I raised his standard outside Nottingham Castle, at the opening of the English Civil War. The stories here are the King, the standard and Henry Ireton, baptised in the town, who fought for Parliament.

groups.title: Holding the castle
groups.intro: From 1643 Colonel John Hutchinson held Nottingham Castle for Parliament. These stories tell of his garrison, of his wife Lucy, who wrote his life, and of the church he had pulled down.

groups.title: Raids, Shelford and the end of the castle
groups.intro: The Royalists of Newark raided the town, Parliament's troops stormed Shelford House in 1645, and in 1651 the castle itself was razed.

layers.title: Frames and lace
layers.intro: How the stocking frame and the lace machine made Nottingham's trade: the inventors, the mills and workshops, the hosiers and lace merchants, and the frame-breakers who fought the machines.

groups.title: Knitting
groups.intro: The county's cloth trades began with wool and the stocking frame, invented at Calverton in 1589, and went on to cotton mills, bleachworks, Luddite frame-breakers and silk.

groups.title: Lace
groups.intro: Lace made Nottingham's fortune in the 19th century, from the Leavers machine and Thomas Adams's warehouse to the big mills of Long Eaton.

layers.title: Risings and riots
layers.intro: When Nottingham rose: a riot over cheese at Goose Fair, the frame-breakers, a march on the town, the Reform riots that burned the castle and a mill, the Chartists on Mapperley Hills, Bulwell's march to save its common, and the riots of 1958.

layers.title: Reform and the vote
layers.intro: Who got a say: the Reform riots of 1831, the Chartists' strike and the election of 1842, the Chartist leader the town elected in 1847, an MP and employer, and the women who campaigned for the vote and first used it in 1918.

groups.title: Reform and Chartists
groups.intro: From the burning of the castle in 1831 to the Chartist by-election of 1842 and O'Connor's win in 1847, men demanded the vote and the right to be heard, until in 1885 the city was given three seats.

groups.title: Votes for women
groups.intro: Women's campaign for the vote came later, and was won in part in 1918.

layers.title: Coal
layers.intro: The pits that dug Nottinghamshire's coal, the wagonway, canal and railway that carried it, and the power stations that burned it.

groups.title: The pits
groups.intro: Collieries and ironworks across the county, from the first sinkings of the 1860s to the closures after the 1984–85 strike. Each shaped a village or a town around it.

groups.title: Carrying the coal
items: The railway that began in a pub
groups.intro: The coal needed carrying: by the wooden wagonway of 1603–04, by canal, by railway, and over the iron viaduct at Bennerley.

groups.title: Power stations
items: The power station that was not built
groups.intro: At the end of the line coal was burned for electricity, from the station at Wilford in 1925 to Ratcliffe-on-Soar, the last coal-fired power station in Britain, which shut in 2024.

layers.title: Railways and roads
layers.intro: How people got about: the railways and their stations, a bridge turned over to cars, the buses and aircraft that came after, and the trams that came back.

groups.title: The railways
items: The railway that began in a pub
groups.intro: Railways reached the county in 1839 and shaped it for a century: stations, viaducts, a great railway yard and the stations that closed.

groups.title: Buses and aircraft
groups.intro: A bus company and two airfields.

groups.title: Trams
groups.intro: Trolleybuses replaced the trams, which left the city in 1936, and ran until 1966; trams returned in 2004, and a depot of 1900 recalls the first ones.

groups.title: Canals and a tunnel
groups.intro: Before railways came the canal; some of its buildings survive, and so does a tunnel meant for carriages.

layers.title: Made in Nottingham
layers.intro: What Nottingham made: Humber's and Raleigh's bicycles and Brough's motorcycles, Player's cigarettes, the medicines of Boots, from Jesse and Florence Boot's shop to ibuprofen, and Paul Smith's clothes.

groups.title: Bicycles and motorcycles
groups.intro: From the 1870s Nottingham and its neighbours made bicycles, and later motorcycles: the Humber works at Beeston, the small workshop in Raleigh Street that became Raleigh, and George Brough's Superior machines.

groups.title: Tobacco
groups.intro: John Player's Castle Tobacco Factories stood in Radford; the bonded warehouses that remain were finished in 1939, and tobacco making in Nottingham ended in 2016.

groups.title: Boots
groups.intro: From a herbalist's shop on Goose Gate in 1849 Boots grew into a great firm. These stories follow the family, the Grade I factories of the 1930s, the Blitz and the making of ibuprofen.

groups.title: Clothes
groups.intro: The county's hosiery firms, and a fashion designer from Beeston who opened his first shop in a tiny room off Byard Lane in 1970, showed his work at the castle in 1995 and designed seating for a Nottingham cinema.

groups.title: Beer, sauce and soap
groups.intro: Basford made things for the kitchen and the bathroom, and brewed: two breweries, a sauce factory and a soap works.

groups.title: Engines and bricks
groups.intro: Heavy industry on the edges of the city: bricks, stone, pots and iron, and the aero engines tested at Hucknall.

layers.title: Markets and fairs
layers.intro: Where Nottingham traded and made merry: the great square and the village markets, the fairs granted by medieval kings and a riot over cheese, and the shops that came after.

groups.title: Markets
groups.intro: The market has always drawn the crowds: at Weekday Cross, then in the Old Market Square, where the Exchange stood from 1726, and in the market towns of the county.

groups.title: Fairs
groups.intro: Charter fairs, among them Goose Fair, which a charter of 1284 mentions, Lenton's horse fair, and a riot at one in 1766.

groups.title: Shops
groups.intro: Shopping moved from Goose Gate to a superstore out of town and a shopping centre in the city.

layers.title: The Victorian town
layers.intro: The town that grew in the 19th century: cemeteries and parks on the hills to the north, a college, theatres and halls, and the architects whose buildings line its streets.

groups.title: Parks and cemeteries
groups.intro: The Victorians laid out public green space: cemeteries, an arboretum and grounds for recreation and sport.

groups.title: Buildings
groups.intro: Buildings of a town grown rich on lace: a warehouse, offices, a hotel, theatres, a music hall and a house.

groups.title: Villages become suburbs
groups.intro: Villages and open fields became suburbs, from the villas of the Park to the railway suburb of Carlton and new housing on the old Clay Fields.

groups.title: Public buildings
groups.intro: The civic buildings of a town that became a city in 1897: a college, a guildhall, a village school and a railway station.

layers.title: Crossing the Trent
layers.intro: Crossing and taming the river: a Roman ford, the ferries, a fort at the bridge, the medieval bridge and its iron successor, the bridges to Wilford and Clifton, the embankment, a flood and the watersports centre.

groups.title: Fords and ferries
groups.intro: Before the bridges the river was crossed by ford and ferry. These stories reach back from a Bronze Age settlement on piles and a Roman ford to Saxon Addensburgh, a ferry at Barton, and the Danes who held Nottingham, against whom a fort was built beside the bridge in the 920s.

groups.title: The bridges
groups.intro: Trent Bridge, the town's crossing, rebuilt after the flood of 1683 and again in the 1860s, and the later bridges upstream and down: the toll and suspension bridges to Wilford, the bridge to Clifton and the railway bridge at Lady Bay.

groups.title: Taming the river
groups.intro: The Trent also flooded, and was walled in and put to use: an embankment, the flood of 1947 and a watersports centre dug from a gravel works.

layers.title: Science and health
layers.intro: Nottingham's scientists, engineers, doctors and nurses: clean water and sewers, a self-taught mathematician, medicines and the MRI scanner.

groups.title: Water
groups.intro: Engineers who brought clean water to the city, and the pumping station that raised it.

groups.title: Science
groups.intro: A miller who became a mathematician, a library, a college built in 1877–81, and the university where magnetic resonance imaging was developed.

groups.title: Medicine
groups.intro: Doctors, nurses and hospitals: the General Hospital of 1782, Nottingham's first woman GP, the making of ibuprofen and the asylum at Mapperley.

layers.title: Soldiers and wars
layers.intro: Soldiers and sailors who lived here, and the two World Wars at home: the munitions works and depots, the airmen and nurses, the bombs and the memorial.

groups.title: Soldiers and sailors
groups.intro: Soldiers and sailors from earlier centuries, the county's own regiment, and a home for the veterans of two Victorian wars.

groups.title: The First World War
groups.intro: A shell filling factory at Chilwell, the explosion of 1918, and how the city remembers those who died in the war.

groups.title: The Second World War
groups.intro: Depots and airfields, bombs on Lady Bay and the Blitz of May 1941.

layers.title: On a plinth
layers.intro: Who Nottingham has put on a plinth, in the order the statues and memorials went up: a Chartist, a regiment, an MP, a queen, an airman, the city's war dead, a hosier, an outlaw and a football manager.

layers.title: Lost Nottingham
layers.intro: Buildings and streets that are gone: pulled down for the Council House, the Victoria and Broad Marsh centres and Maid Marian Way, or burned and closed. Their pins mark where they stood.

groups.title: The town centre
groups.intro: Buildings, streets and a station that the middle of the town has lost, most of them demolished in the 20th century.

groups.title: Industry
groups.intro: Two industrial buildings that no longer stand: a tobacco warehouse and a silk mill.

groups.title: Further out
groups.intro: Lost places beyond the centre: a priory, a church, a hall, a viaduct, a station, a spring and a manor house, and the caves of the Hermitage.

layers.title: Great houses
layers.intro: The halls of the families who owned the land round Nottingham, and the villages and estates they shaped.

groups.title: Clifton and Wilford
groups.intro: On the south bank of the Trent: Clifton Hall with its grove and dovecote, Wilford House and the manor of Wilford, and the West Bridgford estate said to have been won at cards.

groups.title: The south-west and Thrumpton
groups.intro: South-west of the city and up the Trent valley: Chilwell Hall, Ruddington Hall, and Thrumpton Hall, with its staircase, its estate village, the Byrons of Thrumpton and its owners since 1949.

groups.title: East of the city
groups.intro: East of the city: Holme Pierrepont Hall and the Pierreponts, Tollerton Hall, which became a seminary, and Shelford House, stormed in the Civil War.

groups.title: The city and the Park
items: Sold, saved and run by its residents
groups.intro: In and just outside the city: the dukes' mansion on the castle rock, the Park estate that its residents now run, and the hall and grange of Mapperley and Woodthorpe.

groups.title: North and west
groups.intro: North and west of the city: Wollaton Hall, whose restoration Cassandra Willoughby oversaw, Bestwood Lodge, Papplewick Hall and Bulwell Hall.

layers.title: Faith
layers.intro: Churches and chapels from the medieval parish churches to the Methodist missions, and the preachers who founded movements here.

groups.title: Churches
groups.intro: The old and new churches of the city and its near neighbours, from the three mediaeval parish churches and the priory at Lenton, dissolved in 1538, to Pugin's Catholic cathedral.

groups.title: Chapels
groups.intro: Nonconformists, Methodists (in Nottingham from about 1740) and the Salvation Army built chapels and halls of their own, and some of those buildings have since found other uses.

groups.title: Village churches
groups.intro: Each village round the city has its own church, many going back to the 12th and 13th centuries.

layers.title: Women's lives
layers.intro: Nottingham women who campaigned for the vote, ran schools, businesses and libraries, healed, built and wrote.

groups.title: Votes for women
groups.intro: The women who campaigned for the vote in Nottingham, as suffragists and as suffragettes.

groups.title: Work and care
groups.intro: Women who wrote, taught, nursed, built and ran things, from the 17th century to the 20th.

layers.title: Writers and artists
layers.intro: The poets, novelists, painters and photographers who lived, worked or were born here.

groups.title: Writers
groups.intro: Poets and novelists who lived in, wrote of or were born in the county, from Lucy Hutchinson to Alan Sillitoe, by way of Byron and D. H. Lawrence.

groups.title: Artists
groups.intro: Artists who were born or worked here, and an art centre.

layers.title: Sport
layers.intro: Cricket at Trent Bridge, football on both banks of the Trent, prize-fighters, skaters and rowers.

groups.title: Cricket
groups.intro: Trent Bridge grew from a ground behind an inn into a Test ground, and the county's bowlers played their part in Bodyline.

groups.title: Football
groups.intro: Two of the oldest clubs in the country, Notts County and Nottingham Forest, played either side of the Trent, and Forest won the European Cup twice under Brian Clough.

groups.title: Other sports
groups.intro: A bare-knuckle champion, a rowing course, ice dancers and a racehorse.

properties.name: Abel Collin's almshouses
properties.text: Abel Collin, born in Nottingham in 1653, left money in his will of 1704 for almshouses. Those on Friar Lane, built in 1709, were demolished in 1956 to make way for Maid Marian Way; his charity, the oldest in Nottingham, still has houses in Beeston.

properties.name: Trent Bridge cricket ground
properties.text: Arthur Shrewsbury, born in New Lenton in 1856, scored his first century at Trent Bridge in 1876 and captained England seven times, the last professional to do so until Len Hutton. Asked whom he would most like in his side, W. G. Grace said: "Give me Arthur."

properties.name: Trent Bridge cricket ground
properties.text: Bill Voce, born at Annesley Woodhouse in 1909, walked from Hucknall to Trent Bridge hoping for a trial. With Harold Larwood he bowled Bodyline for England, and he later became the county's coach.

properties.name: The Girls' Friendly Society hostel, 4–6 Regent Street
properties.text: From 1913, at the Girls' Friendly Society hostel at 4–6 Regent Street, Constance Penswick Smith (1878–1938) worked to revive Mothering Sunday, with the hostel's superintendent, Ellen Porter.

properties.name: Statue of Feargus O'Connor
properties.text: Feargus O'Connor, the leader of Chartism and owner of its newspaper, the Northern Star, was elected MP for Nottingham in 1847, defeating Thomas Benjamin Hobhouse.[^s1] His statue by J. B. Robinson was put up in the Arboretum in 1859.[^s2]

properties.name: Raleigh Street
properties.text: Frank Bowden took up cycling on his doctor's advice, bought a bicycle from a small workshop in Raleigh Street and in 1887–88 took control of the firm, then making three bicycles a week. He built it into the Raleigh company, and was made a baronet in 1915.

properties.name: Raleigh's Faraday Road works
properties.text: Frank Bowden took up cycling on his doctor's advice, bought a bicycle from a small workshop in Raleigh Street and in 1887–88 took control of the firm, then making three bicycles a week. He built it into the Raleigh company, and was made a baronet in 1915.

properties.name: Brough Superior works
properties.text: George Brough was born in Basford on 21 April 1890 and set up his Brough Superior works on Haydn Road in 1919.[^s1] H. D. Teague of The Motor Cycle called the machines the "Rolls-Royce of Motorcycles".[^s2] T. E. Lawrence owned eight and died of injuries from a crash on the seventh.[^s2] War work ended production in 1940.[^s1][^s2] The pin is approximate.

properties.name: Trent Bridge cricket ground
properties.text: Harold Larwood, born at Nuncargate in 1904, played for Nottinghamshire from 1924 and bowled for England in the Bodyline series. He moved to Australia in 1950; Trent Bridge named the Larwood and Voce Stand after him and Bill Voce in 1985.

properties.name: Wilford village
properties.text: Harry Cursham was born in Wilford on 27 November 1859. In the FA Cup he scored 49 goals in 44 games for Notts County, the competition's individual scoring record, and for England 5 goals in 8 games; he also played two first-class cricket matches for Nottinghamshire. He died on 6 August 1941. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: Wilford village
properties.text: James Iremonger was born in Norton, in the East Riding of Yorkshire, on 5 March 1876, and played for Wilford's football club in 1893.[^s1] He played for Nottingham Forest from 1895 to 1910, won two England caps in 1901–02, played cricket for Nottinghamshire from 1899 to 1914 and coached the county from 1921 to 1938.[^s1] His brother was Albert Iremonger, the Notts County goalkeeper.[^s1][^s2] He died in Nottingham on 25 March 1956.[^s1]

properties.name: Owthorpe
properties.text: Lucy Hutchinson, born in the Tower of London in 1620, was the first to translate the whole of Lucretius into English verse, and her Order and Disorder is perhaps the first epic poem by a woman in English. Her life of her husband, John Hutchinson, written for her family, was printed in 1806. She died at Owthorpe in 1681.

properties.name: 15 Regent Street
properties.text: Margaret Glen-Bott (1891–1969) came to Nottingham in 1916. The first woman gynaecologist to be Honorary Surgeon at the Women's Hospital and the Children's Hospital, and later a magistrate, she lived at 15 Regent Street.

properties.name: Howitt House, South Parade
properties.text: Mary Howitt married William Howitt in 1821, and by 1823 they were living in Nottingham, on Timber Hill, now South Parade, next to Smith's Bank, for over twelve years.[^house] She wrote The Spider and the Fly and translated Hans Christian Andersen's tales.

properties.name: Curzon Street
properties.text: Mary Kendrick, the tidal engineer who led the studies of river levels and silt for the Thames Barrier, grew up on Curzon Street, where her father was a haulage contractor. She later kept the Mersey navigable as its Acting Conservator.

properties.name: Hyson Green
properties.text: In 1877 Mary Potter's Little Company of Mary began in an abandoned factory in Hyson Green. The sisters' main work was caring for the sick and dying. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: The suffragettes' office, Carlton Street
properties.text: Nellie Crocker was the suffragettes' organiser in Nottingham from 1909 to 1912, with an office on Carlton Street. After her eighth arrest, for attacking a post office in London, she spent three months of 1912 in Holloway.

properties.name: 6 Byard Lane
properties.text: Paul Smith was born in Beeston on 5 July 1946. In 1970 he opened his first shop, Paul Smith Vêtements Pour Homme, at 6 Byard Lane, with a floor of only twelve feet by twelve feet. He was knighted in 2000.

properties.name: 18 High Pavement
properties.text: Ruth Bryan (1805–1860) came to Nottingham as a child with her father, a minister. She lived at 18 High Pavement and kept a detailed diary from 1822.

properties.name: Memorial to Samuel Morley
properties.text: Samuel Morley, of the Nottingham hosiery firm I. & R. Morley, was elected MP for Nottingham in 1865 and endowed Morley College in London.[^s1] His memorial by Joseph Else stands at the Arboretum.[^s1]

properties.name: 21 Regent Street
properties.text: Sarah Gray, Nottingham's first woman GP, lived and practised at 21 Regent Street. At the Women's Hospital from 1899 she was refused charge of in-patients; in 1921 she became the first president of the Nottingham Medico-Chirurgical Society.

properties.name: Clifton estate
properties.text: The ice dancers Jayne Torvill and Christopher Dean come from Nottingham.[^s1][^s2][^s3] The square outside the ice centre is named Bolero Square after their Olympic routine.[^s1][^s2][^s3] Jayne Torvill was born in Clifton on 7 October 1957 and worked as an insurance clerk at Norwich Union before skating full-time; at Sarajevo in 1984 she and Christopher Dean won the gold with their free dance to Ravel's Boléro, which earned twelve perfect 6.0 marks.[^s3]

properties.name: Clifton estate
properties.text: Viv Anderson was born in Clifton on 29 July 1956. In ten years at Nottingham Forest, from 1974 to 1984, he played 328 times and won the European Cup twice. In November 1978, against Czechoslovakia, he became the first black footballer to play for England's senior men's team.

properties.name: Howitt House, South Parade
properties.text: William Howitt, born in Heanor, made his home in Nottingham with Mary Howitt and was an alderman of the town, before they moved to Esher in 1837. In 1852 he sailed to Melbourne with two of his sons.

properties.name: Bendigo's tomb
properties.text: William "Bendigo" Thompson, born in Nottingham on 11 October 1811, won the heavyweight championship of England in 1839. He died in 1880 and was buried in St Mary's burial ground, under a tomb with a crouching lion. The city of Bendigo in Australia is indirectly named after him.

properties.name: Mortimer's Hole
properties.text: In 1330 Roger Mortimer, 1st Earl of March, ruled England with Queen Isabella as regents for her young son, Edward III. That October Sir William Montagu led Edward's men up a secret tunnel through the castle rock to a door high in the castle, and they seized Mortimer; he was sent to the Tower of London and hanged a month later. The long passage to the bottom of the rock is known as Mortimer's Hole.

properties.name: Statue of Robin Hood
properties.text: Robin Hood is the legendary outlaw of English folklore, a skilled archer said to rob the rich to give to the poor.[^s1] The earliest ballads are usually thought to be set in the 13th or 14th century, and the first clear mention of Robin Hood rhymes comes in Piers Plowman, in the 1370s.[^s1] In the stories he lives in Sherwood Forest, and his enemy is the Sheriff of Nottingham.[^s1] James Woodford's bronze of him at Nottingham Castle was unveiled in 1952 and listed Grade II in 2018.[^s2]

properties.name: The Exchange
properties.text: When George Larpent resigned his Nottingham seat, Joseph Sturge stood at the by-election: a reformer whose Complete Suffrage Union, a more middle-class rival to the Chartists' own association, campaigned for votes for all men.[^sturge] He lost, and the Conservative John Walter was elected on 4 August 1842; Walter was unseated on petition the next year, and the Liberal Thomas Gisborne won the seat in April 1843. Five years later Nottingham elected the Chartist leader Feargus O'Connor. Where the poll was held is not known.

properties.name: Old Market Square
properties.text: After a poor harvest in 1766, food was dear and people feared shortages. At Goose Fair that October, when Lincolnshire merchants began carting away cheese they had bought, the townspeople tried to stop them; the fair turned to a riot, shops, a warehouse and a boat were looted, and wheels of cheese were rolled down the streets. The mayor could not restore order, and soldiers fired on the crowd, killing William Eggleston, a farmer guarding his own goods. It took several days to bring the town back to order.

properties.name: Old Market Square

properties.name: Statue of Brian Clough
properties.text: Brian Clough managed Nottingham Forest from January 1975 to May 1993.[^s1][^s2] Under him the club won the League in 1977–78 and the European Cup in 1979 and 1980.[^s1] Les Johnson's statue of him, at the corner of King Street and Queen Street, was unveiled by his widow Barbara on 6 November 2008.[^s1][^s2]

properties.name: The Black Boy Hotel
properties.text: A hotel on Long Row, rebuilt in 1886–88 by Watson Fothergill and enlarged around 1900. It was demolished in 1970, and a new shop building, first Littlewoods, went up in its place.

properties.name: The Exchange
properties.text: In 1724–26 the town's Exchange was built in the Market Place to a design by the mayor, Marmaduke Pennell. It held the Corporation's offices, and its Great Hall was used for concerts, elections and balls. It was demolished in 1926 to make way for the Council House.

properties.name: The frame-knitting town
properties.text: After William Lee died in about 1614 the stocking frame spread slowly: in 1644 London had some 400 to 500 frames and Nottinghamshire about 150. In 1728 Nottingham's magistrates refused the authority of the London Company of Framework Knitters, and the town became a chief centre of the trade. England had some 14,000 frames by 1750, and in 1758 Jedediah Strutt's "Derby rib" let them knit ribbing. Short of yarn, the knitters looked for ways to spin cotton here.

properties.name: Saxon Nottingham
properties.text: In 868 a Viking army under Ivar the Boneless and Halfdan Ragnarsson took Nottingham and wintered here. Burgred of Mercia and his West Saxon allies laid siege, but made peace and let them go in 869. From 877 the Danes settled, and Nottingham, a town of about 39 acres, became one of the Five Boroughs of the Danelaw, until Edward of Wessex took it in 918. King Edmund won the Five Boroughs back for the English in 942.

properties.name: Broad Marsh
properties.text: This was boggy ground on the edge of the medieval town, where the Franciscan friary of Greyfriars stood until it was closed in 1539. After large-scale slum clearance, the Broad Marsh shopping centre was officially opened on 25 March 1975. It closed in 2020 and was left partially demolished; caves found beneath it became part of the City of Caves. In 2025 Homes England bought the site to build homes.

properties.name: Drury Hill
properties.text:
The street was first called Vault Lane, after the great rock cellars under the house where it met Low Pavement, and later Parkyn Lane. It took its present name about 1620 from Alderman Drury, a wealthy shoemaker who lived in that house, Vault Hall. Traffic once had to climb the cliff to the old town by Malin Hill, the Long Stairs and Hollow Stone; it found the slope of Drury Hill, up from Narrow Marsh, much easier, and the street became the town's chief business thoroughfare. When carts and carriages came into use in the 17th century it proved too narrow, and Hollow Stone was eased to become a main way into the town.[^old]

At its narrowest the street was only 4 feet 10 inches wide, and a postern gate stood at its top when the town was walled. It was demolished in the 1960s, despite protests, for the Broad Marsh shopping centre.[^lion]

properties.name: Halifax Place Wesleyan Chapel
properties.text: Methodists met in Nottingham from about 1740, in rooms here and there, and in 1782 moved to Hockley Chapel on Goose Gate.[^s1] When the New Connexion split from the Wesleyans in 1797 and took that chapel, the Wesleyans bought land in Halifax Place and opened a chapel for 1,600 on 2 December 1798.[^s1][^s2] Its successor of 1847 had the highest ceiling of any Wesleyan chapel in England; it closed in 1930 and was pulled down in 1966.[^s1]

properties.name: Weekday Cross
properties.text: Before the Old Market Square, Weekday Cross, by the Guild Hall, was the town's main market and its centre. A cross went up here in about 1529–30, and by 1711 people called it "the Pillar". Butter, eggs, pigeons, wild fowl, fruit and fish were sold on Wednesdays and Fridays. The Corporation had the cross pulled down and sold in 1804; Nottingham Civic Society put up a new one in 1993. The Guild Hall's site is now Nottingham Contemporary's.

tree.title: Arboretum plaque for Helen Watts (My Nottingham News, Nottingham City Council)

properties.name: The Arboretum
properties.text: The Representation of the People Act, passed on 6 February 1918, gave the vote to women of 30 and over who met a property qualification, and they voted for the first time on 14 December 1918. That November women had also been allowed to stand for Parliament: in Nottinghamshire the first to do so was Violet Markham, at Mansfield, who lost. In 1919 Bridgid Burke-Bloor became the first woman to stand for Nottingham City Council, and in 1920 Helena Dowson and Caroline Harper were its first women councillors. Women won the vote on the same terms as men on 2 July 1928. A hundred years to the day after that first vote, the city unveiled a plaque by a juniper tree in the Arboretum for the suffragette Helen Watts.[^tree]

properties.name: Church (Rock) Cemetery
properties.text: In 1856 the cemetery, laid out by Edwin Patchitt, was consecrated before it was finished. It is also known as the Rock Cemetery and is listed Grade II*.

properties.name: Forest Recreation Ground
properties.text: Nottingham's racecourse by 1773, and the ground where a club formed in 1865 first played, taking its name from it: Nottingham Forest. Goose Fair has been held here since 1928.

properties.name: General Cemetery
properties.text: In 1836 a cemetery of 18 acres was established at the top of Sion Hill, now Canning Circus, with a gatehouse and almshouses by Samuel Sutton Rawlinson. More than 150,000 people are buried here.

properties.name: Memorial to Samuel Morley
properties.text: Joseph Else's memorial to Samuel Morley, of bronze and stone, stands at the Arboretum's Waverley Street entrance: the hosier who was elected the town's MP in 1865.[^s1] The list of the city's public art dates it to 1928.[^s1] It is listed Grade II.

properties.name: Nottingham Victoria station
properties.text: Nottingham Victoria, the Great Central and Great Northern railways' station, opened on 24 May 1900 and closed on 4 September 1967. It was demolished except for its clock tower, which still stands at the entrance of the Victoria Centre built on the site.

sources.title: List of public art in Nottingham

properties.name: Statue of Feargus O'Connor
properties.text: The stone statue of Feargus O'Connor, by J. B. Robinson of Derby, went up in the Arboretum in 1859: the Chartist leader whom Nottingham had elected its MP in 1847.[^s1] It is listed Grade II.

properties.name: Arboretum Bell Tower
properties.text: The Arboretum's bell tower is a war memorial to the 59th (2nd Nottinghamshire) Regiment of Foot, designed by Marriott Ogle Tarbotton in 1862–63. Its cupola held a bell that British troops took from a temple in Canton during the Second Opium War, until the bell went to the regimental museum in 1956. Two of the cannon beside it were taken at Sebastopol in the Crimean War; the other two are copies.

properties.name: The Arboretum
properties.text: On 11 May 1852 a park laid out under the botanist Samuel Curtis opened here. Its bandstand went up in 1907. The bell from a temple in Canton, taken in the Second Opium War, hung in its war memorial until 1956.

properties.name: Sneinton Hermitage
properties.text: Cave dwellings dug into the sandstone ridge extended out into Sneinton, where they were known as the Hermitage. What little remains can still be seen along Sneinton Hermitage.

properties.name: Sneinton Market
properties.text: In the 1930s the city's wholesale fruit and vegetable market moved here from the Old Market Square.

properties.name: St Ann's
properties.text: On 23 August 1958 a fight in St Ann's grew into a riot between white and West Indian residents; the police restored order within 90 minutes. A crowd of about 4,000 gathered the following weekend. With the Notting Hill riots a week later, the disturbances led to talks between Caribbean governments and the British government. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: Beck Street
properties.text: The building of St Ann's may have begun in about 1750, when Charles Morley, who had been sheriff, made brown earthenware in a small factory on Beck Street; his brown beer jugs sold well. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: St Ann's Well
properties.text: The district takes its name from a spring once thought to heal. It was recorded in 1301 as the Brodewell, and was also called Robin Hood's Well; in 1500 monks built a chapel beside it and dedicated it to St Ann. A spired cover put over it in 1856 was pulled down in 1887 for the railway, and the site was later built over by the Gardeners pub.

properties.name: St Ann's
properties.text: Clearance of the old houses began in 1930, but the war held it up and New Town lasted until 1970, when its Victorian streets were replaced by an estate on the Radburn plan. The film-maker Shane Meadows shot scenes of This Is England here in 2006.

properties.name: Victoria Embankment
properties.text: In 1947 the Trent flooded 3,000 properties, 86 factories and 28 miles of road in Nottingham, and the city's first flood defence was built that year. Photographs of West Bridgford under water are in Inspire Picture Archive. A new defence along 27 km of the river, from Sawley to Colwick, was finished in 2012.

properties.name: Meadow Lane
properties.text: Notts County, called the oldest professional football club in the world, gives 1862 as its foundation, though it was formally organised on 7 December 1864. Its first recorded matches were at the Meadows Cricket Ground, its home until October 1877. It played at Trent Bridge from 1883, and since 1910 at Meadow Lane, on land leased from Nottingham Corporation. In 1894 it beat Bolton Wanderers 4–1 at Goodison Park, the first Second Division team to win the FA Cup. Late in 1901 a set of Notts-style kits sent to Turin gave Juventus their black and white stripes.

properties.name: Meadow Lane
properties.text: Notts County moved here on 3 September 1910. Divided by the Trent, Meadow Lane and the City Ground are the closest pair of football grounds in England.

properties.name: Statue of Queen Victoria
properties.text: Albert Toft's stone statue of Queen Victoria was unveiled in the Market Square in 1905. In 1953 it was moved to the Memorial Gardens on Victoria Embankment, and in 2022 it was cleaned and repaired, its sceptre mended and missing fingers replaced.[^wire] It is listed Grade II.

properties.name: Statue of Robert Juckes Clifton
properties.text: Sir Robert Juckes Clifton, of the Clifton family across the river, was elected MP for Nottingham in 1861 and died of typhoid in 1869, aged 42.[^s1] The Wilford Toll Bridge he had planned opened the next year, and in 1883 William Philip Smith's stone statue of him was put up at its northern end.[^s2] It is listed Grade II.

properties.name: The Meadows rebuilt
properties.text: Much of the Meadows' pre-1919 terraced housing was demolished to make way for a new development of modern council housing, and the viaduct carrying the Great Central railway came down in 1975.

properties.name: Victoria Embankment
properties.text: Between 1898 and 1901 a mile and a quarter of flood defences was built along the Trent under the borough engineer Arthur Brown. Part of it was later laid out as Memorial Gardens to the dead of the First World War.

properties.name: Arkwright's first mill
properties.text: Richard Arkwright's first cotton mill opened in Nottingham in 1768, its machines turned by horses. By 1772 it had four storeys and 300 workers.

properties.name: Hockley
properties.text: From about 1285 the area was known as Walker Gate, after the "walking", or treading, of cloth to thicken it. Nottingham's wool trade mattered: between 1343 and 1345 the price of wool in its market was the standard for all of England.

properties.name: The Park Estate
properties.text: In 1854 the Duke's estate took on the Nottingham architect Thomas Chambers Hine, to design many of the Park's villas. The roads are still lit by gas lamps, believed to be one of the largest such networks left in Europe.

properties.name: Park Terrace
properties.text: The first house in the park, built in 1809 opposite the castle gatehouse, was the vicarage of St Mary's. In 1827 the architect Peter Frederick Robinson published a plan for building over the park, and houses began to go up along Park Terrace in about 1829; within three years there were 40 to 50 of them.

properties.name: The Park Estate
properties.text: The Park began as a wooded deer park on the west side of Nottingham Castle, hunted while the castle belonged to the Crown. In 1663 William Cavendish, 1st Duke of Newcastle, bought the ruined castle together with its park, and the land stayed with his successors for almost three centuries.

properties.name: The Park Estate
properties.text: The Park's villas housed the town's business and public figures: the publisher Richard Allen, who lived at Albert Villa until his death in 1884; the MP Anthony Mundella, for whom Amelia House was built; and Captain Athelstan Popkess, chief constable of Nottingham from 1930 to 1959, at 35 Newcastle Drive.

whenSrc.title: 2A. The Park Estate and Nottingham–Beeston Canal Appendix (transportnottingham.com)

properties.name: British Waterways Building
properties.text: The Trent Navigation Company put up this warehouse at Castle Wharf in about 1919. It later became British Waterways' offices, was converted as part of the Castle Wharf scheme in 1996, and in 2022 was given permission for 95 flats. Which building it was is not certain.

source.title: 2A. The Park Estate and Nottingham–Beeston Canal Appendix (transportnottingham.com)

properties.name: Castle Marina
properties.text: West of the town the canal ran past railway sidings. In the 1980s the sidings were dug out for Castle Marina, a basin of moorings off the canal, with shops and offices round it.

properties.name: The Roman ford
properties.text: In 1900 the remains of a paved Roman ford, edged with oak posts, were found in the Trent at Wilford. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: Captain John Deane
properties.text: In 1710 Captain John Deane's ship, the Nottingham Galley, sank off Boon Island, New England. He later served in the Russian navy under Peter the Great, and in 1736 he retired to Wilford. He is buried in St Wilfrid's churchyard.

properties.name: Wilford village
properties.text: Jeremiah Brandreth, born in Wilford, led the Pentrich rising of 1817 and was known as the Nottingham Captain. He was hanged for high treason outside Derby Gaol that November, and then beheaded.

properties.name: Wilford village
properties.text: Before the Conquest the manor of Wilford belonged to Gode the Countess.[^throsby] In Domesday Book the settlement is named Willesforde, with a fishery, a priest and 23 sokemen. Clifton and Wilford, Peverel lands, passed to the Crown early in Henry II's reign, and the king granted them to Gerbode de Escalt; in Richard I's time they passed to the de Rodes family. Before 1280 Gervase de Clifton obtained both manors from Sir Gerard de Rodes for £30 a year, and a charter of 1280 confirmed the grant.[^wood] In 1853 Sir J. G. J. Clifton was lord of the manor, owned all its land but the church's glebe, and was patron of the church;[^white] in 1870–72 the manor still belonged to Sir R. J. Clifton.[^gazetteer]

properties.name: The old Manor House
properties.text: A house called the Manor House stood here, near the river at the south end of the village green, and is said to have once been a home of the Clifton family. It appears on an 1885 map.[^appendix] Manor House Close was built on its site; next to it stands the only house left of the row once called Manor House and Main Road Cottages.

properties.name: Wilford Crossroads
properties.text: In 1804–05 the young poet Henry Kirke White lived at Wilford Crossroads. He is said to have spent much of his time writing poems in the churchyard, under his favourite tree.

properties.name: Wilford village
properties.text: Wilford parish had 2,769 people in 1891 and about 4,500 by 1901. South Wilford became part of West Bridgford in 1935, and in 1952 Wilford became part of the City of Nottingham. The Silverdale estate was built on its farmland in the late 1950s, and Compton Acres in 1986.

properties.name: Wilford Power Station
properties.text: In 1925 a coal-fired power station opened on the north bank of the Trent. It closed in 1981 and was soon demolished, and the Riverside Retail Park stands on its site.

properties.name: Trent Bridge cricket ground
properties.text: Bodyline, fast bowling aimed at the batsman's body, was England's tactic in the Ashes in Australia in 1932–33.[^s1][^s2] Its bowlers were Nottinghamshire's Harold Larwood and Bill Voce, whom Douglas Jardine met with their county captain, Arthur Carr, to plan it.[^s1][^s2] The uproar ended Larwood's Test career and changed the laws of cricket; Trent Bridge opened the Larwood and Voce Stand in 1985.[^s2]

properties.name: City Ground
properties.text: Under Brian Clough, Nottingham Forest won the European Cup in Munich in May 1979, beating Malmö 1–0 with a goal by Trevor Francis, and again in Madrid a year later, beating Hamburg 1–0 with a goal by John Robertson: back-to-back European Cups.[^s1][^s2]

properties.name: City Ground
properties.text: On 16 April 1898, at the Crystal Palace in south London, Nottingham Forest beat Derby County 3–1. It was the first FA Cup final for both clubs.

properties.text: In 1947 the Trent flooded 3,000 properties, 86 factories and 28 miles of road in Nottingham, and the city's first flood defence was built that year. Photographs of West Bridgford under water are in Inspire Picture Archive. A new defence along 27 km of the river, from Sawley to Colwick, was finished in 2012.

properties.name: The first Test, 1899
properties.text: The first Test at Trent Bridge, England against Australia in June 1899, was W. G. Grace's last Test and Wilfred Rhodes's first.

source.title: Australian cricket team in England in 1899

properties.name: A fort at the bridge
properties.text: Between 919 and 924 Edward the Elder had defences and houses built at the south end of Trent Bridge, to guard Nottingham against the Danes. This was the beginning of West Bridgford. In 1086 the Domesday survey recorded it as part of the manor of Clifton.

properties.name: City Ground
properties.text: Nottingham Forest moved here in 1898, to their seventh home. The name dates from 1897, when Nottingham was granted city status, and Notts County's Meadow Lane is only three hundred yards away, on the other side of the Trent.

properties.name: Compton Acres
properties.text: A district built mostly in the 1990s, named after a garden in Poole. Its tram, opened in 2015, runs along a disused railway line.

properties.name: Edwalton station
properties.text: The station opened in 1880 on the Midland Railway's direct line from Nottingham to Melton Mowbray, which let its London expresses avoid Leicester. It closed to passengers in 1941, and its site is now housing. Beyond it the line became the Old Dalby test track, where the Advanced Passenger Train was tried.

properties.name: The Lady Bay bombs
properties.text: In 1941 a German bomber dropped a line of bombs across Lady Bay. New houses went up on the bomb sites in the 1950s and 1960s, and Pinders Ponds, to the east, are thought to be flooded bomb craters.

properties.name: Trent Bridge cricket ground
properties.text: The first recorded match was played on ground behind the Trent Bridge Inn in 1838, and William Clarke opened the ground in 1841. It hosted its first Test match, England against Australia, in 1899.

properties.name: Won at cards
properties.text: The Musters family gained the West Bridgford estate in 1523, reputedly by winning it in a game of cards. When they sold land for building they set strict rules for it, and the village grew into a suburb, with its own council from 1894 and part of the borough of Rushcliffe from 1972.

properties.name: Bronze Age finds
properties.text: In 1937 finds from a Bronze Age settlement built on piles, from between 1000 and 500 BC, were made near the foot of Clifton Grove. The pin is approximate.

white.title: GENUKI: Clifton, with White's Directory of 1853

properties.name: Clifton Grove
properties.text: A local account says Sir William Clifton planted the avenue of elms in 1677, from a little stone bridge over Fairham Brook up to the hall; it was said to be wide enough for six carriages abreast.[^walk] In 1853 it was "an avenue of trees a mile in length".[^white] By the 18th century the Grove was a favourite outing, and an 1874 guide tells of thousands of Nottingham artisans there at Easter and Whitsuntide.[^walk] The Nottingham poet Henry Kirke White, a butcher's son, published Clifton Grove, a Sketch in Verse, in 1803, aged 17. D. H. Lawrence set a scene of Sons and Lovers (1913) in the Grove.[^walk]

genuki.title: GENUKI: Clifton, with White's Directory of 1853

properties.name: Clifton estate
properties.text: The old village had 381 people in 1801 and 350 in 1911.[^genuki] Planned from 1950, the Clifton council estate was at one time the largest council estate in Europe. Since the 1980s most of its houses have passed into private ownership.

whenSrc.title: Listed buildings in Nottingham (Clifton South ward)

properties.name: George Wells Almshouses
properties.text: Their datestone reads "George Wells, Anno 1709", though Wells's will was written in 1712. The almshouses were for six poor unmarried or widowed women, kept up by his lands in Cropwell Bishop, Wilford and Ruddington, with Sir Gervase Clifton and his heirs as trustees; each woman had an allowance and three tons of coal a year from Clifton Colliery. Restored in the 1970s, they are now two homes.[^walk]

source.title: Listed buildings in Nottingham (Clifton South ward)

properties.name: Clifton Grove
properties.text: A ballad, Bateman's Tragedy, tells of a young man, Bateman, and a beautiful heiress of Clifton who pledge to marry; she breaks her word for a richer widower, and on her wedding day he hangs himself at her door. His ghost haunts her, and in the end carries her off. In the version told locally, the jilted lover drowns himself in the Trent and the bride is dragged into the river at the chasm in the Grove; in another, a Clifton beauty is murdered and thrown down the cliff.[^walk]

properties.name: Barton in the Beans
properties.text: The village's older name was Barton in the Beans, after the beans grown here; fabis is Latin for beans. A ferry crossed the Trent from here to Attenborough from before 1774. Today Fairham, a new district, is being built in the parish beside Clifton.

properties.name: An estate village
properties.text: Up to 1745, John Emerton of Thrumpton Hall built many of the village's gabled brick houses for the estate.

properties.name: The lost church of Flawford
properties.text: St Peter's, the old church of Flawford, closed in 1718 and was pulled down in 1779. Three alabaster figures found in it, probably hidden around 1539, are now at Nottingham Castle Museum, and Ruddington's chapel took its name.

properties.name: Gotham
properties.text: On 2 August 1984 a tornado hit Gotham, damaging buildings but injuring no one.

properties.name: Gotham
properties.text: Gotham means "goat home" in Old English. Washington Irving gave the name "Gotham" to New York in his Salmagundi Papers of 1807, and Bill Finger in turn named Batman's city Gotham City.

properties.name: Gotham
properties.text: Gypsum was dug from Gotham Hill and made into plaster. A branch line about two miles long, opened in March 1899, ran west from the Great Central main line to the works; it closed in the early 1960s and is now a footpath. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: The Wise Men of Gotham
properties.text: The "fools of Gotham" were already mentioned in the fifteenth century, in the Towneley plays.[^s1] A legend says that the villagers played the fool, even trying to fence in a cuckoo, so that King John would build his road and hunting lodge elsewhere.[^s1][^s2] In 1807 Washington Irving called New York "Gotham", and Batman's Gotham City took the name.[^s1][^s2]

properties.name: National Watersports Centre
properties.text: Dug out of a former gravel works, the centre opened in 1971, and hosted the World Rowing Championships in 1975 and 1986. Its whitewater course was built in 1986.

properties.nm: The power station that was not built
properties.name: National Watersports Centre
properties.text: In 1960 the Central Electricity Generating Board proposed a 2,000 MW power station at Holme Pierrepont, with coal by rail and cooling water from the Trent. A public inquiry of 14 days turned it down, partly because it would have shut off the sand and gravel beneath. The gravel was dug instead, and in 1971 the pits became the National Watersports Centre.

properties.name: Shelford Manor
properties.text: In November 1645 Parliament's troops under Sydnam Poyntz, with Colonel John Hutchinson leading the assault, stormed Shelford House, held for the King by Philip Stanhope. About 160 of its defenders were killed, and the house was burnt that night.

dyk.text: The house had been Shelford Priory, founded by Ralph Haunselyn around 1160–80 and granted to Michael Stanhope when it was dissolved in 1536. What survived the fire is now a private house, Shelford Manor.

properties.name: Cotgrave Colliery
properties.text: The colliery came in the early 1960s: from 1962 hundreds of mining families moved here from Radford's closed pit, and the village grew several times over. The pit worked through the 1984–85 strike and closed in 1993.

properties.name: Mill Hill, Cotgrave
properties.text: A 6th-century Anglo-Saxon burial ground has been excavated at Mill Hill, to the north of the old village. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: Player's bonded warehouses
properties.text: John Player built his Castle Tobacco Factories in Radford, and the firm's three bonded warehouses, seven to nine storeys high, were finished here in 1939.[^s1][^s2] Tobacco making in Nottingham ended in 2016; the warehouses were demolished, the last in 2022.[^s1][^s2]

properties.name: Radford
properties.text: Factories, offices and warehouses filled Radford: Raleigh, once the world's largest bicycle maker, and Player's cigarettes among them. By 1891 the parish had 38,718 people, and on 1 April 1897 it was joined to Nottingham.

properties.name: Raleigh Street
properties.text: In 1885 a small bicycle workshop opened in Raleigh Street and gave the company its name; Frank Bowden took it over in 1888.

properties.name: Raleigh's Faraday Road works
properties.text: Alan Sillitoe's 1958 novel became a 1960 film directed by Karel Reisz, with Albert Finney as Arthur Seaton, who works at the Raleigh factory. Much of the exterior location filming took place in Nottingham, and shooting at a Nottingham factory ran two days over schedule and £3,500 over budget.

properties.name: Raleigh's Faraday Road works
properties.text: Frank Bowden took control of a small bicycle maker in Raleigh Street in 1887–88; by 1896 the Raleigh company covered seven and a half acres in Faraday Road.

properties.name: Raleigh's Faraday Road works
properties.text: Alan Sillitoe's 1958 novel became a 1960 film directed by Karel Reisz, with Albert Finney as Arthur Seaton, who works at the Raleigh factory. Much of the exterior location filming took place in Nottingham, and shooting at a Nottingham factory ran two days over schedule and £3,500 over budget.

properties.name: Torvill Drive
properties.text: Coal has always mattered in Wollaton, from the wagonway onwards. Wollaton Colliery closed in 1965, and houses now cover its ground and that of the old canal: the Torvill and Dean estate. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: Wollaton Wagonway
properties.text: In 1603–1604 Huntingdon Beaumont and Sir Percival Willoughby laid a wooden wagonway from the Strelley coal pits to Wollaton Lane End, its wagons drawn by horses. It is described as the first railway in Britain.

properties.name: Lowe's Silk Mill
properties.text: During the Reform riots of 1831, Lowe's Silk Mill in Beeston was burnt on 11 October, the day after Nottingham Castle, and the same day the riots ceased.

properties.name: National Shell Filling Factory
properties.text: Viscount Chetwynd built the factory from 1915 to fill shells with explosive; it filled some 19 million during the First World War. On 1 July 1918 eight tons of TNT exploded, killing 134 people. The site is now Chetwynd Barracks.

properties.name: Chilwell village
properties.text: The Charlton family, after whom the Charlton Arms is named, lived at Chilwell Hall, since pulled down. In 1906 Chilwell Manor Golf Club was laid out on land that had belonged to the manor, and the Manor House and Chilwell Green stood until 1965.

properties.name: Chilwell village
properties.text: Roman buildings, pottery and coins have been found in Chilwell. It began as a hamlet on the road from Nottingham to Ashby-de-la-Zouch, and is in the Domesday Book of 1086. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: Wilford village
properties.text: On the night of 9–10 June 1817, men from around Pentrich in Derbyshire set out from South Wingfield to march on Nottingham, led by Jeremiah Brandreth, the Nottingham Captain. At Giltbrook they met a small force of Light Dragoons and scattered. The news that had set them marching was a hoax by William Oliver, a government informer; Brandreth and two others were hanged and beheaded at Derby.

properties.name: Giltbrook
properties.text: On the night of 9–10 June 1817, men from around Pentrich in Derbyshire set out from South Wingfield to march on Nottingham, led by Jeremiah Brandreth, the Nottingham Captain. At Giltbrook they met a small force of Light Dragoons and scattered. The news that had set them marching was a hoax by William Oliver, a government informer; Brandreth and two others were hanged and beheaded at Derby.

properties.name: Giltbrook Viaduct
properties.text: Between May 1873 and November 1875 Joseph Firbank built a viaduct here for the Great Northern Railway, 43 arches and 1,716 feet long, known locally as Forty Bridges. It was pulled down in 1973 to make way for the A610 bypass.

properties.name: Giltbrook
properties.text: Giltbrook's name is thought to come from the Old English Gylden Broc, the golden brook, after the stream that runs down from the fields north of where IKEA now stands. A retail park was built beside IKEA in 2008.

credit.author: Tim Heaton

properties.name: Attenborough village
properties.text: In Saxon times the village was known as Addensburgh, and a ferry crossed the Trent here from before 1774. In 1966 a hoard of Roman coins was found on a footpath near the railway and Barrett Lane.

properties.name: Stapleford Cross
properties.text: The Anglo-Saxon cross in St Helen's churchyard dates from around AD 1000, though some put it as early as the 8th century.[^s1] Its shaft is carved with interlace and a winged figure with a spear, perhaps an archangel or St Luke.[^s1] Its head was lost in the 18th century; after several moves it came to the churchyard in 1928.[^s1] Pevsner called it by far the most important pre-Conquest monument in Nottinghamshire, and it is listed Grade I.[^s1][^s2]

credit.author: Jeff Tomlinson

properties.name: Hemlock Stone
properties.text: The Hemlock Stone is a pillar of red Triassic sandstone, more than 200 million years old, on the hill above Stapleford. A hard cap of barytes protected its top while water, ice and wind wore away the softer rock beneath. Stories have grown round it: Beltane fires lit on it into the 19th century, witches and hemlock, a giant who threw it, and the Devil, who flung it at Lenton Priory, where it fell short.

properties.name: Arnold Market
properties.text: Arnold was a town of hosiery factories, and in 1968 it gained its own market in the town centre.

properties.name: Arnold
properties.text: Domesday Book, in 1086, calls the village Ernehale. A history of Arnold written in 1913 traces the name back to its Anglo-Saxon settlers, worn down over the centuries into Arnold.

properties.name: The first Luddites
properties.text: The Luddite movement began in Arnold on 11 March 1811. Across Nottinghamshire the frame-breakers went after the "wide" knitting frames used to make cheap goods.

properties.name: Calverton Colliery
properties.text: Calverton Colliery was officially opened on 24 September 1952, and the village grew from 1,304 people in 1951 to 5,658 in 1961. British Coal shut the mine on 19 November 1993; it worked again under RJB Mining until it closed for good in April 1999. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: The stocking frame
properties.text: In 1589 William Lee of Calverton invented the stocking frame, a machine that knitted. Legend has it that Elizabeth I refused him a patent. The trade grew here, and from 1728 Nottingham was one of its main centres.

properties.name: Gedling Colliery
properties.text: Gedling Colliery opened in 1899 and was the area's main employer for almost a century.[^s1][^s2] In the 1960s it dug over a million tonnes of coal a year with 1,400 men, about one in ten of them from the Caribbean, and was known as the "pit of all nations"; 128 men died there over its life.[^s1] It closed in 1991, and in 2015 its grounds opened as Gedling Country Park.[^s1][^s2]

properties.name: Gedling House Woods
properties.text: The woods and meadows of Gedling House are owned by the borough council and cared for by a friends' group. The woods became a local nature reserve in 1992, and the meadow joined them in 2007. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: Hucknall tram stop
properties.text: Trams returned to Nottingham after 68 years when the Nottingham Express Transit network opened in 2004.[^s1] Hucknall's stop opened on 9 March 2004 with the rest of the first phase, beside the station reopened on 17 May 1993 as part of the Robin Hood Line.[^s2]

properties.name: Hucknall
properties.text: Domesday Book, in 1086, calls it Hochenale. From 1295 until 1915 the town was Hucknall Torkard, after the Torcards, the leading landowners.

properties.name: Former Hucknall Colliery site
properties.text: Hucknall had been a village of framework knitters. In 1861 the Hucknall Colliery Company sank its Top Pit off Watnall Road, and in 1866 its Bottom Pit off Portland Road, and in under a century Hucknall grew into a market town. The Top Pit closed in 1943 and the Bottom Pit in 1986. A mining memorial in the town centre names both pits. The pin on the former colliery site is approximate.

properties.name: Hucknall Mining Memorial
properties.text: Hucknall had been a village of framework knitters. In 1861 the Hucknall Colliery Company sank its Top Pit off Watnall Road, and in 1866 its Bottom Pit off Portland Road, and in under a century Hucknall grew into a market town. The Top Pit closed in 1943 and the Bottom Pit in 1986. A mining memorial in the town centre names both pits. The pin on the former colliery site is approximate.

properties.name: Hucknall aerodrome
properties.text: The airfield opened in 1916, and from 1927 Rolls-Royce used it to test its engines. In the Second World War the first P-51 Mustang fitted with a Rolls-Royce Merlin flew from here, and in December 1940 a German prisoner, Franz von Werra, tried to escape by posing as a Dutch pilot and taking a Hurricane. In the early 1950s the works built the "Flying Bedstead", a test rig for vertical take-off, whose first free flight was on 3 August 1954. The flight test centre closed in 1971. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: Basford
properties.text: Domesday Book, in 1086, calls the village Baseford; the name holds that of an Anglo-Saxon called Basa. It became part of Nottingham in 1877.

properties.name: Basford
properties.text: In 1836 the young Nottingham poet Philip James Bailey went to live at his father's house in Old Basford to write. The result was Festus, a vast poem on the Faust story published in 1839, which Tennyson admired.

properties.name: New Basford
properties.text: Basford made things for the kitchen and the bathroom. The grocer F. G. Garton started a pickle and sauce factory near his home on Sandon Street and registered the name HP Sauce in 1895. Gerard Brothers opened a soap works in the 1890s; Cussons took it over in 1955, and it closed in 2005. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: Basford
properties.text: The Leen's clean water brought the bleachers. A directory of 1853 counted eight bleaching works in Basford, with many stocking frames and bobbin-net machines, and a population that had grown from 2,124 to 10,093 by 1851.

properties.name: Bulwell
properties.text: Domesday Book, in 1086, records Bulwell as the village of Buleuuelle. The name probably comes from a spring, the Bull Well, or from an Anglo-Saxon man called Bulla and his well.

properties.name: Bulwell Hall Park
properties.text: The landowner John Newton built Bulwell Hall in 1770. It was sold at auction in 1864 to Samuel Thomas Cooper, and was pulled down in 1956; its grounds are now Bulwell Hall Park.

properties.name: Bulwell Market Place
properties.text: A local law of about 1320 said that only those with covered premises could trade, so Bulwell's market grew up with stalls that were covered while in use and opened out when not. The Market Place has kept much of its old shape.

properties.name: Bulwell
properties.text: Bulwell's limestone was quarried for building. Stretches of the wall round Wollaton Hall, built in the late 16th century, are of Bulwell stone.

properties.name: Bulwell
properties.text: Victorian Bulwell lived by the Leen. Glove-making, begun in about 1840, employed some 700 people until 1864, and by 1853 there were three bleachworks along the river.

properties.name: Bulwell Bogs
properties.text: The Bogs, the wet meadow by the Leen, were common land. When the lord of the manor tried to enclose them in 1872, about a thousand people marched on the land to claim it,[^bogs] and the Corporation later bought it for the town. The park won a Green Flag Award in 2004.

properties.name: Sherwood
properties.text: Mansfield Road was the main road from London to Yorkshire, and a turnpike from 1787. Samuel Hall laid out Sherwood's first streets beside it in 1825; the road was paved and lit in 1879, the year horse trams arrived.

properties.name: Mapperley Hills Common
properties.text: In August 1842 a meeting of more than two thousand in the Market Place voted to stop work until the People's Charter became law. The magistrates banned further meetings, and for days troops and police broke up gatherings across the town. On 23 August Chartists from Hucknall, Bulwell, Arnold, Basford and other places met on the common on Mapperley Hills; the 2nd Dragoon Guards were sent, and when the crowd, sitting on the grass to eat, would not disperse, Colonel Rolleston had about four hundred arrested. As they were marched into the town, a crowd stoned the soldiers and police. About fifty went for trial, some getting hard labour. Afterwards the town's workers turned instead against the Corn Laws and the price of bread. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: Mapperley
properties.text: In the 1790s Ichabod Wright built Mapperley Hall at the heart of his estate. His grandson, Colonel Charles Ichabod Wright, began selling land for houses in 1873, but most of the estate was released only in 1903; some 163 houses were approved in Mapperley Park between 1906 and 1914.

properties.name: Mapperley Plains
properties.text: The clay of the high ground fed some of the area's biggest brickworks. In the 1860s Edward Gripper mechanised them, with Hoffmann kilns, and brickmaking went on until 1969.[^walk] Mapperley bricks are said to have built St Pancras station, and so, people said, Nottingham once stood on Mapperley Plains. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: Mapperley
properties.text: The name goes back at least to the 14th century. Thomas Mapurley was under-sheriff of Nottinghamshire from about 1387 and mayor of Nottingham in 1402–03. The high ground to the north-east was long known as Mapperley Plains.

properties.name: Carlton
properties.text: The textile trade and the railways grew Carlton in the 19th century: its population climbed steadily from the 1840s, and by 1850 it had become a suburb with its own houses, churches and schools. The tram line from Nottingham reached it in 1914.

properties.name: Carlton
properties.text: Domesday Book, in 1086, calls it Carentune. For centuries it was a small township in the manor and parish of Gedling, home to farmers and framework knitters.

properties.name: King George V Recreation Ground
properties.text: The King George V Recreation Ground on Standhill Road was once the Standhill Brickworks.

properties.name: Long Eaton Market Place
properties.text: Long Eaton stayed a village until the Midland Counties Railway came in 1839. A great railway yard, Toton Sidings, grew up just north of the town, and by 1900 it had more than 10,000 people.

properties.name: Long Eaton Market Place
properties.text: Lace made Long Eaton. High Street Mill dates from 1857, West End Mill of 1882 stands beside the Erewash Canal, and by 1907 the town had almost 1,400 lace machines and more than 4,000 people in the trade.

properties.nm: The Great Fire of Long Eaton
properties.name: Long Eaton Market Place
properties.text: In 1694 the "Great Fire" of Long Eaton destroyed 14 houses and several other buildings in the market place.

properties.name: Ilkeston Market Place
properties.text: Henry III granted Ilkeston its charter in 1252, and its fair is held in the Market Place. Two fairs were joined into one in 1888, and the Charter Fair has been held every October since.

properties.name: Ilkeston station
properties.text: Ilkeston once had three stations. The Town station closed to passengers in 1947, the North in 1964 and the Junction in January 1967, leaving the town without a station for fifty years. After a long campaign a new Ilkeston station was approved in 2013 and, delayed by flood works and great crested newts, opened on 2 April 2017. The pin is approximate.

properties.name: Ilkeston
properties.text: Ilkeston was probably founded in the 6th century, and is said to take its name from a founder called Elch. Domesday Book, in 1086, calls it Tilchestune, held mostly by Gilbert de Ghent. Queen Victoria made it a borough in 1887.
